bio.heading: Biodiversity baseline and monitoring
bio.intro: Diversity of the living collection per bed and garden, from the current plant records, with vegetation from very high resolution satellite images. For KPI reporting, not daily maintenance.

t.evennessSub: mean per bed, 1 = all species equally common
t.betaSub: mean Sørensen, 0 same species, 1 none shared

bio.method: Computed in the platform from the living plant records: each record is one plant and every plant counts through its bed (Terra Garden baseline study method). Per bed: species, plants, Shannon, Simpson, inverse Simpson, Pielou evenness, Margalef and Hill numbers; between beds: mean Bray-Curtis, Jaccard and Sørensen dissimilarity with Simpson turnover and nestedness. Verified identical to the R packages vegan and betapart on the same data.
bio.methodMore: Richness estimation follows Chao et al. (2014) for abundance data (Chao1, sample coverage, interpolation and extrapolation to twice the sample; equal to iNEXT). The spatial pattern is Moran's I with queen contiguity (bed corners within 1 m), row-standardised weights and 999 permutations (equal to spdep moran.mc). The ordination is a principal coordinates analysis of Bray-Curtis. Biomass uses life-form coefficients per plant with lognormal spread; plants are treated as independent.

rich.heading: How many species are there?
rich.title: Species against plants sampled
rich.dashed: Dashed: estimated beyond the plants recorded
rich.chao1Sub: lower-bound estimate of the true number
rich.coverageSub: share of plants whose species is already recorded

ord.title: Beds by species composition
ord.help: Each dot is a bed; beds close together have similar species (principal coordinates of Bray-Curtis). The percentages are the share of variation each axis shows.

moran.heading: Are similar beds next to each other?
moran.clustered: neighbouring beds are more alike than by chance
moran.few: Only {{n}} of {{beds}} beds touch another bed (within 1 m); read with care
moran.help: Moran's I compares each bed with the beds touching it. Above the expected value means neighbours are alike; p is the share of 999 random shuffles that give an I as large.

help.s: How many different species grow in the bed.
help.n: How many plants are recorded in the bed.
help.shannon: Richness and balance together: higher when there are more species and none dominates.
help.evenness: How equally the plants are shared among the species (0 to 1; 1 = all equally common).
help.hill_q1: The number of equally common species that would give the same diversity (an 'effective' species count).
help.species_density_ha: Species per hectare of bed: richness adjusted for bed size.
help.pct_native_species: Share of the bed's species native to the Arabian Peninsula and nearby arid regions.
help.mean_sorensen: How different the bed is from the other beds (0 = same species, 1 = none shared). High = distinctive bed.
help.carbon_t_ha: Carbon stored in the bed's plants and roots per hectare (indicative coefficients).
help.sat: Average of the satellite layer over the bed: higher = greener, more vigorous vegetation.

s.text: The number of different species in a bed, a garden or the whole site. The simplest measure of biodiversity.

n.text: The number of plants recorded. Richness depends partly on it: more plants usually means more species.

shannon.text: Combines richness and evenness. Rises with more species and with plants spread evenly over them. Typical garden beds: 1 to 3.

simpson.text: The chance that two plants picked at random are different species (0 to 1). Less sensitive to rare species than Shannon.

evenness.text: Shannon divided by its maximum for that number of species (0 to 1). 1 means every species is equally common; low values mean one or two species dominate.

margalef.text: Richness corrected for the number of plants, (S - 1) / ln N, so beds with different plant counts compare more fairly.

hill.text: Diversity as an 'effective number of species': q0 counts all species, q1 weighs them by abundance (exp of Shannon), q2 counts only the common ones (inverse Simpson).

density.text: Richness divided by bed area, to compare small and large beds.

native.text: Species whose natural range includes the Arabian Peninsula and nearby arid regions, matched on the distribution text from the plant database. A broad match that may over-count.

threatened.text: Species listed by the IUCN as Critically Endangered, Endangered or Vulnerable.

beta.text: How different two beds are in species (0 = identical, 1 = nothing in common). Bray-Curtis also uses plant counts; Jaccard and Sørensen use presence only. The map shows each bed's average against all others.

turnover.text: The two parts of Sørensen dissimilarity: turnover means beds hold different species; nestedness means one bed holds a subset of another's species.

chao1.text: An estimate of how many species there really are, including ones not yet recorded, from the number of species with one or two plants. A lower bound.

coverage.text: The share of plants whose species is already in the records (Good-Turing). Near 100% means few species are missing.

curve.text: How the species count grows as more plants are recorded (solid), and the expected count if twice as many were recorded (dashed). A flattening curve means most species are already known.

ordination.text: Beds placed on a plane so that beds with similar species sit close together, from the Bray-Curtis dissimilarity. The axis percentages show how much of the variation each axis captures.

moran.text: Whether beds that touch have similar values. Above the expected value (about 0) means neighbours are alike; p is the chance of a pattern this strong by random arrangement.

carbon.text: Dry weight of plants and roots from life-form averages, times 0.47 for carbon, and x 44/12 for CO2. Indicative: assumes mature plants and unverified coefficients.

ndvi.text: Normalised difference vegetation index from red and near-infrared light (-1 to 1). Over about 0.2 means living vegetation; higher means denser, more vigorous plants.

greenness.text: A vegetation index from the visible colours only, for images without near-infrared. Weaker than NDVI; shown on vegetation-coloured pixels only.

stress.text: A bed much less green than the typical bed on that layer. It flags beds to check; it is not a measurement of water or plant health.

change.text: Vegetation in Feb 2025 compared with Oct 2026 on the satellite images: red lost, blue new. Exploratory: confirm on site.

water.heading: Water requirement
water.intro: Crop water demand per bed by the FAO-56 method against the current flat irrigation rate, a satellite proxy of water stress, and metered use once flow meters report. For KPI reporting, not daily maintenance.

t.underSub: demand above the flat rate in at least one month
t.noMeters: No flow meters yet: demand is estimated, not measured

chart.title: Garden water per day: FAO-56 demand and the flat rate

water.stressHelp: A visible or near-infrared greenness proxy compared across beds. Low greenness can mean too little water, but also young planting, pruning, bare mulch or succulents; check on site.
water.method: FAO-56: ETc = Kc × ET0. Kc per bed is the mean, over its plants, of the Kc of their life form (from the Hortis life forms); gross demand = ETc / drip efficiency × bed area, per month with the monthly ET0 (Terra Garden baseline study method). Compared with the flat rate per m² every day. The parameters below are all unverified.
water.meters: Measured use will come from flow meters registered as assets of type Flow meter in a bed; their readings arrive with the sensor module (Phase 4). Until then every bed shows Not metered.

help.demand_month: Water the bed's plants need per m2 per day in the chosen month (FAO-56, with drip losses).
help.demand_year: Water the bed needs in a year, in m3.
help.saving: How much less water the FAO-56 demand needs than the current flat rate (negative = the flat rate is too low).
help.kc: Crop coefficient: the bed's water use relative to reference grass, from its plants' life forms.
help.months_under: Months in which the flat rate gives less water than the plants need.
